name: Duff in the Army
description: Recently Duff has been a soldier in the army. Malek is her commander. Their country, Andarz Gu has n cities (numbered from 1 to n ) and n - 1 bidirectional roads. Each road connects two different cities. There exist a unique path between any two cities. There are also m people living in Andarz Gu (numbered from 1 to m ). Each person has and ID number. ID number of i - th person is i and he/she lives in city number c i . Note that there may be more than one person in a city, also there may be no people living in the city. Malek loves to order. That's why he asks Duff to answer to q queries. In each query, he gives her numbers v , u and a . To answer a query: Assume there are x people living in the cities lying on the path from city v to city u . Assume these people's IDs are p 1 , p 2 , ..., p x in increasing order. If k = min ( x , a ) , then Duff should tell Malek numbers k , p 1 , p 2 , ..., p k in this order. In the other words, Malek wants to know a minimums on that path (or less, if there are less than a people). Duff is very busy at the moment, so she asked you to help her and answer the queries.
input_specification: The first line of input contains three integers, n , m and q ( 1 ≤ n , m , q ≤ 10 5 ). The next n - 1 lines contain the roads. Each line contains two integers v and u , endpoints of a road ( 1 ≤ v , u ≤ n , v ≠ u ). Next line contains m integers c 1 , c 2 , ..., c m separated by spaces ( 1 ≤ c i ≤ n for each 1 ≤ i ≤ m ). Next q lines contain the queries. Each of them contains three integers, v , u and a ( 1 ≤ v , u ≤ n and 1 ≤ a ≤ 10 ).
output_specification: For each query, print numbers k , p 1 , p 2 , ..., p k separated by spaces in one line.
approach_summary: Build a Segment Tree over the array. Implement point update and associative range query operations in O(log N) time per query.

topic_editorial.title: Editorial: 587C — Duff in the Army [57. Segment Tree (Point Update Range Query)]
topic_editorial.summary: Range queries and updates via Segment Tree.
topic_editorial.key_invariant: The query operation is associative (e.g., sum, min, max, gcd). Any contiguous range $[L, R]$ can be decomposed into at most $O(\log N)$ canonical dyadic intervals represented by nodes in a binary tree.
topic_editorial.solution_walkthrough:
### Step 1: Tree Construction
We build a binary segment tree over array $A[1..N]$.
Each node covers a segment $[L, R]$. If $L = R$, the node stores $A[L]$. Otherwise:
$$\text{node.val} = \text{combine}(\text{left\_child.val}, \text{right\_child.val})$$

### Step 2: Point / Range Updates
To update position $pos$ with value $val$:
- Traverse down to the leaf node $[pos, pos]$.
- Update leaf value.
- Recompute ancestor values on the way back up in $O(\log N)$ time.

### Step 3: Range Query Processing
To query the associative aggregate on range $[qL, qR]$:
- If current segment $[L, R]$ is completely within $[qL, qR]$, return node value.
- If disjoint, return identity element.
- Otherwise, split and return $\text{combine}(\text{query}(left), \text{query}(right))$.
topic_editorial.complexity_analysis:
- **Time Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}((N + Q) \log N)$
  Building the segment tree takes $\mathcal{O}(N)$. Each point/range query and update traverses at most $4 \log N$ tree nodes, requiring $\mathcal{O}(\log N)$ time per query.
- **Space Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(N)$
  A standard binary segment tree requires at most $4N$ nodes to represent elements up to index $N$.
